title: 3 new Talbot Board of Ed members sworn into roles
content: Cynthia Jurrius, Ann O'Connor, and Karla Wieland-Cherry were sworn in as new members of the Talbot County Board of Education on December 18, 2024. O'Connor (District 2) and Wieland-Cherry (District 5) won their seats in recent elections, while Jurrius (District 6) took office in November.

title: Budget discussions kicked off at Talbot Board of Ed work session
content: The Talbot Board of Education discussed preliminary budget considerations at a work session on December 18, 2024, as planning for the fiscal year 2026 budget is underway. Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones outlined priorities including academic equity, student engagement, and staff recruitment and retention. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi mentioned special education as a recent focus area. The district needs to make shifts in two programs to comply with Blueprint requirements, which affect funding for smaller schools.

title: CBMM summer camp registration opens Jan. 2 for members
content: CBMM summer camp registration opens on Jan. 2, 2025, with a two-week sign-up period exclusively for members. Registration for eight weeks of camps begins on Jan. 16, and will be open to non-members thereafter. CBMM offers various camps, including Sea Squirts (ages 4-6), Terrapins (grades 1-3), Summer Workshop (grades 4-6 & 6-9), Museum Masters (grades 4-6), and Inspiration Chesapeake (grades 6-9) camps, with tuition ranging from $165 to $375 per week.

title: St. Michaels' Classic Motor Museum donation campaign for new property
content: The Classic Motor Museum in St. Michaels, MD is seeking $300,000 in donations to complete its $1.2 million goal for a property extension by Jan. 17, 2025. The non-profit organization aims to provide hands-on experiences for students of the Automotive Technician Apprenticeship Program. The program began in 2022 and has gathered over $900,000 in donations so far, with Gina Verhalen as administrator. The museum plans to renovate the property to include a '50s style gas station and classroom learning space.

title: 'Rare birds': Apprentices learn the boat building ropes at CBMM
content: Kaeo Clarke and Carstan Gage graduated from CBMM's state-accredited Shipwright Apprenticeship program on December 19, 2024. Kaeo is a native of Annapolis who completed his apprenticeship after working on the Maryland Dove build and Winnie Estelle refit. Carstan is from Oregon, made the cross-country move to CBMM in August 2022, and focused on maintaining CBMM's floating fleet. Both logged 4,000 hours of hands-on experience and skill development training under CBMM staff.

title: Talbot Board of Ed votes in Jackson as president, Dodson as vice president
content: The Talbot County Board of Education re-elected Emily Jackson as president and Amy Dodson as vice president during Wednesday's meeting on December 20, 2024. Jackson was nominated by the nominating committee and has been a board member since 2018. Dodson assumes the role previously held by Candace Henry and represents District 3.

title: Talbot leaders optimistic about improvements at Easton Middle, across TCPS
content: Talbot County Board of Education officials are optimistic about improvements made at Easton Middle School, which saw a year-to-year drop in its star rating from three to two stars due to a decrease in school quality and student success points. The Maryland Department of Education's report showed small increases in academic achievement and English proficiency, but not enough to counter the drop in student attendance, which contributed to the decline. Easton Middle School is taking steps to address chronic absenteeism, with efforts led by Principal Kelly Murdoch and supported by teachers, social workers, and administrators. The district is also assessing school performance internally, celebrating growth at Easton Middle and other schools, rather than relying solely on external ratings.

title: Talbot Board of Ed voices mixed opinions over 2025-26 calendar draft
content: Talbot County Board of Education members voiced mixed opinions on a draft calendar for the 2025-26 school year. The draft included two days off in March and a five-day spring break from April 2 to April 6, 2026. Helga Einhorn presented the draft, which sparked confusion among board members, including Emily Jackson, who called it "surprisingly contentious." Board President Emily Jackson expressed support for extending spring break, while Deborah Bridges liked the two days off in March.

title: Lockerman Middle School celebrates new STEM Center
content: Lockerman Middle School in Denton, MD, celebrated its new STEM Center with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on December 23, 2024. A $500,000 grant from the Cal Ripken, Sr. Foundation funded the center, providing students with resources such as 3D printers, coding robots, and electronic kits. The University of Maryland Medical System partnered with the foundation to support the initiative. The school's superintendent, Derek Simmons, and principal, Jeannine Necessary, praised the grant for bringing unique opportunities to Lockerman students.

title: Beloved bus driver 'Mrs. Dea' brings holiday cheer to young passengers
content: Nedean Crawford, known as "Mrs. Dea," is a beloved bus driver in Cecil County, Maryland, who has been driving for 28 years and averages around 61 students per semester. She makes an impact on many lives as a positive female role model, greeting each student entering and leaving the bus daily, and spending extra time getting to know them. Mrs. Dea's route includes Elk Neck Elementary, North East High School, and their Twilight program for students who need extra help, and she is known for her holiday cheer, decorating her bus with lights, garland, and singing festive songs with her students.

title: Fifth-grader recognized with Hero Award for saving classmate's life
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

James Phillips, a fifth-grader, received a Hero Award for potentially saving his classmate's life in the cafeteria at Conowingo Elementary School on December 11. Dr. Jeffrey Lawson, Cecil County Public Schools Superintendent, honored Phillips for his bravery and dedication to helping others. The incident occurred during lunch when one student started choking, and Phillips performed the Heimlich maneuver successfully.

title: Miles River Yacht Club's Annual Angel Tree event brings holiday joy
content: The Miles River Yacht Club's Annual Angel Tree event brings holiday joy to the Eastern Shore, providing gifts and essentials to over 30 local children through collaboration with Head Start of Shore Up and the Benedictine School. Nick Simpson, commodore at the yacht club, said this event showcases the club's mission statement and generous characteristics. The program, which has been running for over a decade, identifies children in need and distributes gifts and clothing items to families in need.

title: Classical charter school looks to open in Queen Anne's
content: A proposed classical charter school in Queen Anne's County aims to open in the fall of 2026. The school, called Queen Anne's Classical Charter School (QACCS), is a tuition-free pre-K through eighth grade school that will provide an alternative educational approach. QACCS was founded by Audrey Scott and local parents with the goal of improving student performance and character.

title: State eyes new way to count students in need
content: Maryland is examining its poverty count method in public schools, led by Comptroller Brooke Lierman, due to undercounting of students in need. A new study aims to address this issue, which disproportionately affects immigrant students. The state currently relies on proxy measures like Medicaid and SNAP eligibility to calculate aid for schools. A new data set from 2013 is being proposed, but many public schools have closed since then. The results will be presented by Dec. 1, 2025, with recommendations to the Maryland General Assembly.

title: Maryland stories: This reading club is going to the dogs
content: Southern Maryland-based Pets on Wheels, a program started by Johns Hopkins in 2013, uses therapy animals to help homebound patients feel less lonely and improve reading skills and literacy for children and adults alike. The program was recently visited at the Leonardtown Library and has been praised for its benefits, including increased confidence and calmness. The organization is led by Coordinator Sharon Stapf and relies on volunteers who must meet specific pet qualifications, including the "canine good citizenship test."

title: Chesapeake College works to become Hispanic-Serving Institution
content: Chesapeake College aims to become a Hispanic-Serving Institution. Zulema Delacruz Martinez, a 2024 graduate and founder of the Hispanic/Latino Student Union, credits TRiO programs for her success. The college has seen a 64% increase in its Hispanic population over the last decade, with over 90% of attendees at FAFSA Nights applying to Chesapeake College. Zulema Delacruz Martinez was awarded the John T. Harrison Award and stated that she wants to help other students from similar backgrounds succeed.

title: Foundation of HOPE moves toward goals in the new year
content: The Foundation of HOPE, an Easton-based nonprofit, held a gala/luncheon on December 14 to celebrate its accomplishments and share goals for the upcoming year. The foundation, founded in 2018 by Keasha Haythe, aims to empower women and girls in the Eastern Shore through after-school classes covering topics such as workforce development and low self-esteem. Over $150,000 was received from the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development in December, launching a capital campaign for the foundation's headquarters. The program now serves over 100 students and hopes to grow to include 30 students by 2025.

title: Schools to remain closed Friday
content: Talbot County Public Schools and Caroline County Public Schools announced closure on January 10 due to inclement weather, the fifth day of closure, which may impact spring semester academic calendar. Dorchester County Public Schools students will have a virtual instruction day instead.

title: Biden Hall: UD planning social sciences building named after U.S. president
content: The University of Delaware is planning to build an interdisciplinary social sciences building named after Joseph R. Biden, Jr., with construction expected to begin in 2025. The new facility will be located on the main campus in Newark and will house the Joe Biden School of Public Policy & Administration and the Biden Institute. The project has received $20 million in state funding from former Governor John Carney and is scheduled for design and programmatic planning in the 2025 calendar year.

title: Phone pouches improving student focus, discipline in Caroline, district says
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Caroline County Public Schools implemented an experimental pilot program using Yondr's cellphone pouches to keep students off their phones during school hours. The first semester showed pleasing results, with increased attentiveness, reduced cyberbullying incidents (21% reduction), and improved pass rates. The program aims to expand to ninth graders in future years, but officials will weigh the pros and cons before making a decision. Some parents have expressed concerns about not having direct communication with their children, while students have tried to tamper with or break into their pouches.

title: Talbot Board of Ed sees initial budget proposal
content: The Talbot Board of Education reviewed its proposed $85.8 million budget for fiscal year 2026 on January 15, 2025. The draft budget totals $8.6 million more than fiscal year 2025 and includes increases in fixed charges, instructional salaries, and other instructional costs. Anticipated grant funding is expected to be $9-10 million, but less than last fiscal year due to the state's education initiative, Blueprint for Maryland's Future. The proposed budget includes 33 additional positions, including six English for Speakers of Other Languages teachers, coaches, or assistants.

title: Talbot Board of Ed adds makeup day for snow; approves 2025-26 calendar
content:
Here is a concise summary of the article:

The Talbot County Board of Education added a day to the end of this year's school calendar due to the snowstorm in January 2025. The board unanimously approved an adjusted calendar with students' last day on June 13 and teachers' last day on June 16. In choosing the district's 2025-2026 calendar, the board voted 6-1, with Wieland-Cherry dissenting, to adopt a draft with two days off in March and a five-day spring break, with amendments including it as part of inclement weather days.

title: Educators need to return to basics
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Gov. Moore postponed implementing Blueprint for Maryland in schools due to a $2.7 billion deficit.
The Talbot Board of Education plans to implement Blueprint despite opposition, with an $8.6 million increase to the school budget.
Maryland's students have low proficiency rates in English language skills (60%) and mathematics (17.2%).
The author criticizes "equity in math" as promoting feelings rather than mastery, calling for educators to return to basics.
Gov. Moore postponed Blueprint implementation due to a $2.7 billion deficit, but the Talbot Board of Education is still planning to implement it despite opposition.

title: Caroline schools closed, Talbot schools on delay
content: Caroline County Public Schools closed January 21, 2025; Talbot County Public Schools operate on two-hour delay that same day. Offices remain open for both school districts, while Dorchester County Public Schools are unaffected.

title: Local school districts affected by PowerSchool data breach
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

School districts in Caroline, Dorchester, and Talbot counties were affected by a data breach involving PowerSchool in late December 2025. PowerSchool notified the districts on January 7 that personal information such as names, dates of birth, medical info, and social security numbers had been obtained by hackers. The companies involved have enhanced their security protocols and committed to providing credit monitoring services for two years to affected individuals.

title: Dorchester BOE recognizes student contest winners
content: The Dorchester County Board of Education recognized three winners of the Superintendent's Holiday Card Contest for 2024: Adalynn Haugh (Vienna Elementary, 2nd grade), Kali Johnson (Hurlock Elementary, 3rd grade), Elisabeth Claggett (North Dorchester Middle, 8th grade) and Adrien Sinkeldam (North Dorchester High, 10th grade). The contest is held annually to showcase students' artistic talents.

title: Critchlow Adkins cuts ribbon on new offices in downtown Easton
content: Critchlow Adkins Children's Centers held a ribbon-cutting ceremony for its new central office building in downtown Easton on January 24, 2025. The nonprofit was previously located on Washington Street but purchased a 15 S. Hanson St. building after the town approved a development at their previous site. Criticlow Adkins will use the new offices as a hub for its five child care centers across the county, hosting meetings and bringing staff together.

title: Dorchester County Public Schools faces budget deficit
content: Dorchester County Public Schools is facing a $10.19 million budget deficit for fiscal year 2026 due to expected revenues of $86 million and estimated expenses of $97.5 million. The district's superintendent, Jymil Thompson, attributes the deficit to fixed costs and unfunded mandates from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, passed in 2021. The district has taken initial actions to reduce the deficit, including reducing staff positions and non-essential spending. The school board will host additional budget work sessions on February 13 and March, and seeks public input to inform their decision-making process.

title: TCPS superintendent addresses immigration enforcement concerns in letter to families
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi wrote a letter to staff and families stating that schools are "safe places" for all students, staff, and families. The letter came after President Donald Trump's inauguration, which led to sweeping policy changes in federal immigration enforcement. A directive from the Trump administration reversed a policy protecting areas like schools, churches, and shelters from immigration enforcement. Pepukayi assured parents of her district's commitment to providing a welcoming and supportive learning environment for all students regardless of their background or immigration status.

title: After 116 years, 'Junior Naval Academy' closes its doors
content: Leonard Hall Junior Naval Academy closed its doors on February 4, 2025, after 116 years in operation. The school had eight students who are now attending other schools. A lease was not signed due to challenges and low enrollment, despite efforts to find a solution. In January 2024, the St. Mary's County commissioners decided not to ratify the school's lease.

title: Eastern Shore legislators discuss education funding and county burdens
content: Eastern Shore legislators discussed education funding and county burdens on February 8, 2025. Local government research manager Hiram Burch outlined how local governments will assume $144 million of state budget gaps in fiscal year 2026, including a $970,000 projection for Queen Anne's County. Gov. Wes Moore's administration touted record education funding, but many legislators questioned whether it was mandated by the state's funding plan, The Blueprint, under former Gov. Larry Hogan. Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes stated that special education funding would remain unaffected by proposed cuts to the Developmental Disabilities Administration.

title: Caroline schools closed, Talbot and Dorchester remote Wednesday
content: Talbot and Dorchester county school campuses will be closed on February 12 due to inclement weather, with students attending school virtually. Caroline County schools are also closing on February 12, but will not have a virtual learning day.

title: Caroline County Public Schools could face major state budget cuts
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

Caroline County Public Schools may face $41 million in state funding cuts over eight years due to Gov. Wes Moore's proposed budget. Superintendent Derek Simmons stated that while the district will be "OK" in FY26, long-term cuts will add up. The proposed budget includes reductions in foundation funding ($868,273), compensatory education ($513,912), and multilingual learners' funding ($91,425). Foundation funding declines are projected to be $25.6 million over eight years, while compensatory education and multilingual learners' funding declines will total $13.5 million and nearly $2.5 million, respectively.

title: Talbot school leaders discuss immediate, long-term effects of Blueprint cuts
content: Talbot County Public Schools may face a $1.7 million funding gap in fiscal year 2025 due to cuts in The Blueprint for Maryland's Future. Governor Wes Moore proposed the Excellence in Maryland Public Schools Act, which could reduce Talbot County's funding by $685,000 in fiscal year 2026. The district anticipates cumulative reductions of $30 million over eight years if the bill is passed. District Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi and Board Member Amy Dodson criticized the proposals, citing the impact on compensatory education and multilingual learners funding.

title: Talbot Board of Education approves FY2026 budget
content: The Talbot County Board of Education approved the FY2026 unrestricted budget at $86 million, with an $8.9 million increase from last year's $77.1 million. The budget includes $2 million for 33 new positions and $1.3 million in health insurance cost increases due to inflation. A public hearing will be held in May after the district presents the budget to the Talbot County Council next month. The district is seeking $18.4 million in capital funding, primarily for renovations at Chapel District Elementary School and new stadium lights at St. Michaels Middle High School.

title: Talbot Board of Ed discusses dress code, school uniforms
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

The Talbot County Board of Education discussed dress code updates and the possibility of implementing school uniforms during its virtual meeting on February 14, 2025. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi revised the district's administrative regulations to remove specific language targeting certain clothing items, citing discrepancies in enforcing dress code standards. Board Member Ann O'Connor expressed support for implementing school uniforms, saying they would "put everyone on the same playing field" and solve problems, while Board Vice President Amy Dodson mentioned her positive experience with uniforms at a past high school. The board plans to gather community input and historical context before making a decision on implementing school uniforms.

title: Open Doors Partners in Education continues support of literacy
content: Open Doors Partners in Education continues to provide free and low-cost tutoring and literacy support, with over 50 attendees at its open house on February 3, 2025, in Chestertown. The organization, led by Executive Director Ashley Singer, utilizes the Orton-Gillingham approach, a multi-sensory approach designed to help struggling readers. Open Doors has 57 students enrolled and was recognized as Organization of the Year in 2023 by Kent County Chamber of Commerce.

title: Chesapeake Culinary Center offers education everyone
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

The Chesapeake Culinary Center offers education programs for people of all ages, focusing on healthy eating and budgeting. David Murray, operations manager and head chef, started his culinary career in Caroline County and now teaches at the center, which serves the community that raised him. The center offers a range of classes, including workshops and mini-series, with topics such as meal prep, preserving food, and cooking skills for kids. Plans are to expand the center's offerings outside of Caroline County into other areas of the Eastern Shore, including bartending and serving courses.

title: Open house, open doors, open minds and hearts
content: Open Doors Partners in Education, a non-profit organization, was founded in fall 2020 and has provided tutoring and literacy support to over 100 individuals in Kent County and surrounding communities since its opening. Executive Director Ashley Singer hosted an open house event at their center on February 1, 2025, which attracted over 50 attendees including board members, staff, students, and donors. The organization utilizes the Orton-Gillingham approach, a multi-sensory method to help struggling readers. As of 2022, they had enrolled 57 students with instruction provided at no cost or low cost.

title: Dorchester County Public Schools credits test improvement to student accountability
content: Dorchester County Public Schools reported a significant improvement in reading proficiency for Mace's Lane Middle School eighth graders, with a 20.8% increase from the beginning of the year assessment. Reading and Language Arts Supervisor Laura Aberg attributes this change to students taking a reading diagnostic seriously. The school saw notable increases in other schools as well: North Dorchester Middle (1.1%), South Dorchester School (4%).

title: Thousands of Maryland students are chronically absent each year
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Maryland students face high rates of chronic absenteeism, with nearly 27% of students missing 10% or more of school in the 2023-2024 year, an increase from 2018. Baltimore City has the highest chronic absenteeism rate among Maryland jurisdictions, with nearly half of all public school students chronically absent last year. Effective strategies to combat absenteeism include attendance contracts, parent conferences, and incentives like gift cards or snow tubing trips. State education leaders aim to reduce chronic absenteeism rates to 15% by next school year through initiatives such as creating a chronic absenteeism task force and developing a toolkit to address student absenteeism.

title: Bringing history alive: 9th annual GES Wax Museum honors leaders in African American history
content: The ninth annual Living Wax Museum was held at Grasonville Elementary School on February 21, 2025, where 75 fourth-graders recreated influential African American figures as living wax figures. Students studied prominent figures in African American history throughout February, including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Serena Williams.

title: St. Michaels students advocate for new illuminated sign
content: St. Michaels Middle High School students Phoebe Cole and Kyle Murphy advocated for an illuminated sign outside the school in February 2025. The Commissioners of St. Michaels introduced an ordinance to allow the school to have an illuminated sign, which would bring more attention to events and announcements. The town officials suggested changing the ordinance name from "educational facilities" to "public school" to allow other event announcements. A public hearing was scheduled for a second meeting in March 2025.

title: 2025 senior scholarship application open
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

The Peoples Bank, Fleetwood Insurance Group, and BGV Insurance are offering a $6,000 scholarship fund for graduating seniors in Kent, Queen Anne's, and Talbot Counties. The scholarship program is open to students from these counties, with no residency requirements. Applications must be submitted by May 1 through the provided website or email/ mail address. Funding will support college, university, or trade school tuition.

title: Easton, Kent Island High National Honor Society groups hosting talent show for charity
content: The Kent Island High School and Easton High School National Honor Society chapters are hosting a charity talent show on March 12, 2025, at Kent Island High School auditorium to raise money for For All Seasons' rape crisis center. Myiah Barnard and Gabriella Streaker, presidents of the NHS chapters, are spearheading the event.

title: Post Labor Day start slated for Caroline 2025-26 school year
content: Caroline County Board of Education members voted for a post Labor Day start date for the 2025-2026 school year. The first day of school is set for Tuesday, September 2, 2025, with teachers returning to school on August 25. The county has three inclement weather days accounted for in the new calendar, following four used last year for snow.

title: Mid-Shore program aims to teach kids about health care careers
content: Three Mid-Shore women - Dr. Judith Gieske, Ruth Ann Jones, and Cynthia Watson - are launching "Introduction to Careers in Healthcare" (ITCH), a program to introduce the next generation to the healthcare industry on the Eastern Shore.

title: Easton High School takes home ACE Mentor Program gold cup
content: Easton High School won the gold cup at the ACE Mentor Program of Maryland's Eastern Shore awards ceremony on March 12, 2025, for its project to create a multimodal transportation station in Annapolis. Rachael Whiting, vice chair and lead mentor, said the projects also included St. Michaels Middle High School's arcade and mini golf, and Saints Peter and Paul High School's train station connecting Maryland and Delaware. Easton High School engineering teacher Nicholas Werner received the ACE Community Award. The program aims to connect high school students with professionals in design and construction.

title: Dorchester County Blueprint costs higher than 2022 projections
content: Dorchester County's projected education expenses have increased from $23.9 million in 2022 to $26.3 million for fiscal year 2026, a decrease of $2.4 million. The county expected to owe $26.8 million in fiscal year 2030 and now expects to spend $36.3 million on education in fiscal year 2034, up from $29.4 million previously estimated.

title: Caroline County discuss Chesapeake College at first FY26 budget workshop
content: Caroline County Commissioners discussed funding for Chesapeake College's proposed rebuilding of Queen Anne's Tech building at their first FY26 budget workshop on March 19, 2025. The project is a state-funded initiative with counties contributing to its cost; three counties must approve the new building. Caroline County will contribute $2.7 million over three years, with most funding coming in fiscal year 2027-28. Chesapeake College President Clifford Coppersmith expects the state to cover 75% of costs. The commissioners decided to table the discussion until the end of the budget workshop.

title: Community school leaders in Talbot County aim to make a difference
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Katie Fox and Shelby Parks lead community schools at Easton Elementary and Easton Middle in Talbot County, MD, respectively, providing resources for students in need since 2019. The two schools aim to increase availability of healthy foods, provide mental health resources, and add enrichment programs, despite uncertainty over future funding due to the state's $3 billion deficit. Despite this, the district is moving forward with implementing community school programs, including partnering with Choptank Community Health. Easton Elementary received "per-pupil" funding in its third year, supporting before- and after-school programs, while Easton Middle is focusing on mental health, food insecurity, and transportation challenges.

title: Dorchester County Council, Board of Education discuss budget concerns
content:
Here is a concise summary of the article:

The Dorchester County Council and Board of Education discussed budget concerns for fiscal year 2026, citing state mandates affecting budgets. The school district reduced its estimated budget deficit from $10.19 million to $5.59 million since January. DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson presented the draft budget on March 18, while Board of Education member Chris Wheedleton and Vice President Talibah Chikwendu discussed potential implications.

title: CTE students house at Chesapeake College
content: CTE students at Queen Anne's County High School collaborated with Chesapeake College to build a mock house in the Tech Building from February to March 2025. The project, led by Carpentry Instructor Ron Frederick, taught students carpentry and masonry skills while framing real-world experience. Students gained knowledge in multiple trades, including electricity, plumbing, and HVAC, under the guidance of Queen Anne's County High School career coach Betsy Ricketts.

title: What it was like ... to be a teacher
content: Tamara Forte was a first-grade teacher in her 15th year when COVID-19 prompted changes to teaching methods and classrooms. In March 2020, teachers were told to close schools for two weeks, then later had to send learning packets home with limited control over their instruction. Teachers adapted to virtual learning, conducting Zoom calls, troubleshooting internet issues, and sending inspiring messages to students. When fall returned, teachers prepared materials for at-home use, spaced desks 6 feet apart, and simultaneously taught in-person and at-home students before rotating schedules allowed students to return to school in a limited capacity.

title: Schools struggle to bridge learning gaps, adapt to a new normal
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Queen Anne's County Public Schools Superintendent Patricia Saelens emphasized the district's focus on tutoring, academic intervention, and social-emotional strategies to address learning gaps. Chronic absenteeism remains above 25% across Mid-Shore counties, with Queen Anne's at 22.9%, while virtual learning faces challenges due to technology access disparities. Despite setbacks, educators see lasting benefits from pandemic-related changes, including increased proficiency with technology and innovative approaches like student support coaches. Students who graduated during the pandemic are now succeeding in academics and careers, proving their resilience. The Mid-Shore school districts continue to navigate post-COVID realities with a focus on adaptation and social-emotional development.

title: Easton Middle administrators: New cell phone restrictions are working
content: Easton Middle School administrators reported a positive impact from new cell phone restrictions implemented in December 2024, citing improvements in student engagement and safety. The school piloted the Yondr system, which requires students to place their phones in locked pouches throughout the day. Administrators discussed potential expansion of the policy to other schools and acknowledged research showing negative effects of excessive cell phone use on mental health starting at upper elementary levels.

title: DCPS looks to staff reductions to balance budget
content: Dorchester County Public Schools is considering staff reductions due to a $5.59 million deficit for fiscal year 2026. DCPS Superintendent Jymil Thompson aims to reduce staff by 12-24 positions to save between $900,000 and $1.8 million. The district is reviewing attrition rate trends and will negotiate with staff representatives to potentially save an additional $3.5 million.

title: Teacher for a Day brings community into the classroom
content: Community members participated in the "Teacher for a Day" event at schools across Cecil County Public Schools from March 3 to 13. Business leaders like Josh Hayhurst of Superdojo Martial Arts and Nick LaBrant with Utilitrain visited schools, observing classes and teaching lessons on topics such as math, reading, and power lines. The initiative aimed to showcase the work of educators and connect community members with students and teachers, with participants praising the experience's positive impact on students and faculty.

title: Caroline County Public Schools announce finalists for Teacher, Support Employee of the Year
content:
Caroline County Public Schools announced finalists for Teacher of the Year and Support Employee of the Year: 
Support Employee of the Year Finalists: Jenn Claytor, Chadney Ennals, Donna Fazenbaker, Desiray Korell, Nick Marshall.
Teacher of the Year Finalist: Lisa Dayton, Andrew Buffenmyer, Tom Cheezum, Kimberly Mielke, John Moyer III.

title: Plan to require school uniforms doesn't gain traction with Talbot Board of Ed
content: Talbot County Public Schools Board of Education failed to advance a proposal for school uniforms, with nearly 1,900 community survey responses recording 49% in favor and 45% opposed. The proposal was made by Board member Ann O'Connor, who suggested that after one year, there could be a "hand-me-down" uniform shop. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi shared the results of the survey, stating that implementing uniforms would be an expensive undertaking and potentially requiring assistance for low-income families.

title: Elks National chief spotlights community impact in regional meet
content: The Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks hosted its Maryland, Delaware and District of Columbia regional conference March 21-23 on Kent Island. National leader Douglas A. Schiefer was a keynote speaker with the theme "Elkdom's HEART for America." The local lodge has donated over $100,000 annually to charities, including the National Cancer Society and Boys & Girls Scouting programs. Douglas A. Schiefer is the Grand Exalted Ruler from Bucyrus, Ohio, while Angela Meyer is the current president of the Maryland, Delaware and DC area.

title: Amid budget woes, Dorchester cancels summer school, appeals to students to 'get the work done'
content: Dorchester County Public Schools will not offer summer school in 2025 due to budget restraints. President Sheri Hubbard said there is still time for students at risk of repeating a grade to improve their grades and avoid retention. The district faces a $5.59 million deficit and plans to reduce staff by 12-24 positions. Superintendant Jymil Thompson advised parents to plan accordingly if their child is failing a course, as summer school will not be available.

title: Education workers empty their offices after recent layoffs
content: Education workers in the US Department of Education packed up their desks after layoffs aimed at reducing the workforce by 50% due to a "reduction in force" process that bypassed seniority and performance-based rankings. The layoffs began with approximately 2,200 employees receiving early buyouts or retirements, leaving around 1,300 employees subject to layoff notices. Former employees gathered outside the department's headquarters in solidarity, protesting what they called an "assault on public education." Demonstrations grew from a small gathering at the Office of the State Superintendent of Education to a larger event at the Department of Education's headquarters.

title: Committee made for potential new Lockerman Middle School
content: A committee called the Education Specifications Committee was formed in April 2025 to discuss renovating or replacing Lockerman Middle School in Easton, Maryland, as part of Caroline County Public Schools' 2024-2026 construction project. The committee is led by Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons and includes stakeholders from schools, community members, and state officials. Consultant David Lever will use the committee's documents to design the school, which would receive $76 million in funding from the state, with the county responsible for the remaining 11%.

title: Talbot County wrestles with schools funding request, long-term Blueprint concerns
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Talbot County Council voted not to include an additional $5.7 million in funding for Talbot County Public Schools in the fiscal year 2026 budget. The county's draft budget already includes around $55 million in required education funding as mandated by The Blueprint for Maryland's Future. Superintendant Sharon Pepukayi said the district will have to prioritize and make tough decisions if the county only provides the minimum required funding. A joint meeting found common ground on long-term sustainability of the state's Blueprint initiative, with officials agreeing it will take time and strategic planning to meet the increasing funding requirements set by 2034.

title: Lauren Rose named TCPS Teacher of the Year. Giovanni Wynn is Support Staff of the Year
content: Lauren Rose was named TCPS Teacher of the Year and Giovanni Wynn was named Support Staff of the Year. They were honored at the Talbot Stars celebration on April 3, 2025, at the Easton Elks Lodge. Lauren Rose is band director at Easton High School, while Giovanni Wynn is family service coordinator at the St. Michaels Judy Center.

title: QA Teacher of the Year is Marcie Mamas
content: Marcie Mamas, a business teacher at Kent Island High School in Stevensville, MD, was named Teacher of the Year for the 2025-2026 school year. Mamas is entering her 29th year in education and hopes to inspire students to discover their passions and develop real-world skills. She will represent Queen Anne's County Public Schools as Teacher of the Year, a title she expressed overwhelming gratitude for.

title: University of Delaware asks state for $43.5 million to build Biden Hall, renovate labs
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

The University of Delaware is requesting $43.5 million from the state legislature for capital projects, including building Biden Hall and renovating aging laboratories. The university is asking for $20 million to build Biden Hall, an interdisciplinary social sciences building named after former President Joe Biden, with a focus on technology and academic growth. UD is also seeking $20 million to address deferred maintenance of its laboratories and other buildings, which have accumulated a backlog of $1.2 billion in needed repairs and upgrades. The university's remaining request of $3.5 million will go towards renovating lab and classroom space in Georgetown and Lewes.

title: Maryland wrestles with blow to the state schools budget
content: Maryland lawmakers scramble to adjust education budget after federal funding of $418 million may not come through as expected. Senate President Bill Ferguson says state had already spent approximately $300 million and allocated rest to school districts. Senate Republicans propose cuts, including pausing implementation of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future plan for two years. Sen. Mary Beth Carozza introduces amendment to Excellence in Maryland Public Schools Act to pause plan due to "obvious accountability issues."

title: Chapel District Elementary renovations nearing 30% completion mark
content:
Here is a summary of the article:

Construction teams at Chapel District Elementary School are making progress on renovations that began in summer 2024 and are expected to take about two years to complete. The project has spent around $11.28 million, or 30% of its total cost, with approximately $27 million in county funding and state funds from Maryland's Interagency Commission on School Construction. Director Kevin Shafer noted the construction was started 34 days late due to septic system issues, but credits project manager Bill Stagg for getting the project back on track. The school's renovations will add around 16,000 square feet of learning space and include a new media center and playground renovation.

title: Freedom of speech under assault on campuses
content: Columbia University expelled, suspended, and revoked degrees of students accused of peaceful protest against pro-Palestinian speech in 2025. The Trump administration rescinded $400 million in federal funding for such speech. President George H.W. Bush launched Operation Desert Storm in 1991, leading to the bombing and slaughter of retreating Iraqi troops and civilians. The US has continued to wage war since then, with the current Gaza genocide protests sparking debate over free speech.

title: Four months in, Easton Middle staff, parents weigh in on cell phone pouches
content: Easton Middle School staff and parents weigh in on cell phone pouches implemented since December 2024, with principal Kelly Murdoch saying students are less distracted during instruction. Talbot County acquired Yondr pouches from companies like Caroline and Dorchester districts. Parents Carla Beavers and Nicole Crosby have mixed opinions, with Beavers' son focusing more on school instruction after leaving his phone at home. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi says the policy could be expanded to other schools in 2026, but opinions are "mixed" among students.

title: Schools face shortage of social workers
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Jaden Smith, a second-year master's student in social work at Howard University, works as a school social worker at Bard High School Early College DC in Washington D.C. Project PRESS, a pilot program launched in 2023, aims to increase and diversify the school social work labor force nationwide, particularly in underserved communities. The program, which received a $2.6 million federal grant, has placed 22 second-year master's students in schools in the nation's capital, including Wards 7 and 8. Project PRESS focuses on culturally responsive training, trauma-informed care, and creating treatment plans for students with socio-emotional challenges.

title: Speakers ask to keep St. Mary's elementary music and arts intact
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

Speakers at a St. Mary's school board meeting on March 26 expressed concerns about scaling back elementary music and arts programs. A proposed three-year plan would transition from a 10-day rotation cycle to a four-day cohort model, allowing students to participate in one ensemble during special area music time. The new model aims to "enhance the quality of instruction" but some speakers warned it could cause inequity and negatively impact vulnerable learners. Some schools, like Green Holly Elementary, have been using the cohort model for 10 years, with data showing a reduction in pullouts, referrals, suspensions, and ISI incidents.

title: Caroline County Board of Ed declares last day of school, discuss virtual instruction
content: The Caroline County Board of Education declared June 17 as the last day of school due to inclement weather closures exceeding four days allotted. The board concluded that conducting virtual instruction on inclement weather days would be challenging and likely unfeasible. Factors considered include ensuring student internet access, providing necessary devices and translation services for multilingual learners, special education students, and homeless students. The estimated cost to provide the required devices was approximately $736,000 for students and $35,000 for teachers over five years.

title: Rescinded federal reimbursements cause $1.4 million impact on TCPS health center
content: The TCPS health center in Easton, Maryland has been delayed due to rescinded federal reimbursements from the U.S. Department of Education. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon announced on March 28 that the department would not honor extension requests for projects granted pandemic-era funds. The decision puts over $400 million of Maryland schools' funding at risk. Remaining costs for the health center total around $1.4 million, with TCPS having paid $127,000 to Marathon Health so far.

title: Maryland will slow – not stop – its investment in schools
content: Maryland lawmakers passed a revised education reform plan, freezing annual funding increases for students in poverty, special education, and English language learners. The bill, initially introduced by Gov. Wes Moore in January 2025, made marginal cuts instead of dramatic rollbacks proposed earlier. Funding increases under the Blueprint were deemed too crucial to pause, but the most major cuts targeted the collaborative time initiative for teachers. The bill passed with "no" votes from Republican lawmakers, citing financial burden concerns.

title: Buffenmyer, Marshall named Caroline Teacher, Support Staff of the Year
content: Andrew Buffenmyer was named Teacher of the Year and Nick Marshall was named Support Staff of the Year at a ceremony held by Caroline County Public Schools in Ridgely, Maryland. The award winners will represent the district in state contests: Buffenmyer in the state's Teacher of the Year contest and Marshall is already planning to continue his work.

title: Cell phone pouches coming to St. Michaels Middle next year
content: The Talbot County Board of Education voted unanimously to introduce cell phone pouches at St. Michaels Middle School for the 2025-2026 school year. A similar program has been piloted at Easton Middle School since December, with improved student engagement and a decrease in bullying reported. The board will not implement pouches at high schools next year but may consider it in the future due to differing opinions on its effectiveness. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi estimated a cost of $9,000 for the program, while Board member Karla Wieland-Cherry suggested it could cost around $38,000 if expanded to high schools.

title: 'We can turn lightbulbs on'
content: A program called Introduction to Careers in Healthcare (ITCH) is launching in Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties, aimed at sparking interest in healthcare careers from middle school through high school. Dr. Judy Gieske leads a team of retired health care professionals along with volunteers in the initiative. Construction on a new medical facility in Talbot County has begun, but skilled staff are needed to fill the expected 2028 opening. The program's goals include introducing healthcare careers early and reconnecting the hospital with the community. ITCH aims to build a homegrown workforce supporting local students.

title: Maryland State of Reading Report: 'time for a comeback after a decade of decline'
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 sentences:

Maryland's reading achievement has shown incremental gains, but a new report reveals that 67% of fourth-grade students and nearly two-thirds of eighth-grade students cannot read at a proficient level. The Maryland READS "State of Reading in Maryland 2025" report calls for a comprehensive approach to literacy, prioritizing teacher training, community-driven efforts, and addressing excessive screen time. Trish Brennan-Gac, executive director of Maryland READS, criticized recent legislation for missing the mark on funding for literacy coaches. State leaders have taken steps toward a solution, but more work is needed to address the state's reading crisis. The report underscores that a deep and lasting crisis remains despite progress.

title: High school graduation rate reaches seven-year high
content: Maryland's high school graduation rate reached 88% in 2024, its highest point since 2017, according to the Maryland State Department of Education. The increase is significant among student groups that faced barriers to graduation, including Hispanic students and multilingual learners. Talbot County had a graduation rate of 95%, while Caroline and Dorchester counties fell below the state average. The Blueprint for Maryland's Future education reform law aims to close equity gaps, with several strategies aligning with recent progress.

title: College built as an economic engine for Shore
content: Chesapeake College was founded in December 1965 as a community college to address regional economic and workforce needs on Maryland's Eastern Shore. The college is part of the American Dream concept, connecting individuals to jobs and education. Gov. Wes Moore visited the Wye Mills campus in April 2025 with Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller and Secretary Sanjay Rai to highlight Chesapeake's role as a regional hub. The college has since become a workforce champion, supporting students and the local economy with innovative training facilities and programs.

title: Church Hill Park welcomes StoryWalk
content: Queen Anne's County Library welcomed a new StoryWalk at Church Hill Park on April 22, 2025, in collaboration with county parks and recreation. The library, along with funding from United Way of Queen Anne's County and Friends of the Library, made it possible. Other locations for StoryWalks include Route 18 Park in Centreville and Sudlersville Park.

title: Tilghman Island celebrates opening of Judy Center
content: Tilghman Island's Judy Center opened in January 2025 and is serving 40 families, providing workshops, family support services, and more for children up to five years old. The center is Talbot County's third location, following Easton and St. Michaels, and aims to ensure young children and families become comfortable in a school environment. Lori Julian, the center's coordinator, joined local officials and staff to cut the ribbon on April 24, 2025, marking a significant step toward closing gaps for local families.

title: 'Open up worlds': Donor gifts $1 million to BAAM girls program
content: Dr. Eileen Amy Ryan donated $1 million to Building African American Minds (BAAM) on April 25, 2025. The gift will expand BAAM's girls program at the middle-school level. BAAM is a nonprofit organization based in Easton, Maryland, led by Executive Director Dina Daly.

title: ‘Catastrophic’: Could Trump 'defund" Head Start preschools program?
content: Jennie Mauer, executive director of the Wisconsin Head Start Association, is concerned about a looming "chaotic disaster" due to potential funding cuts under President Trump's austerity efforts. The program, established in the 1960s, provides free preschools to over 800,000 lower-income children nationwide and has faced delays in funding and potential elimination. U.S. Sens. Patty Murray (D-WA) and Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) have expressed concerns about Trump's administration defunding Head Start. The program employs over 250,000 staff across the country and advocates fear it would have severe economic tolls on working-class families.

title: Maryland graduation rates hit 88% in '24 a seven-year high
content: Maryland's high school graduation rate reached 88% in 2024, a seven-year high since 2017, with significant gains among Hispanic and multilingual learners. The state's education department reports a nearly full-point jump in overall graduation rate, including increases of over seven percentage points for Hispanic students and more than ten percentage points for multilingual learners. Anne Arundel County Public Schools reported a 89% graduation rate, with six schools increasing by two or more percentage points. Maryland is implementing the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, which aligns with areas of progress in the graduation data. Theresa Timmons Parrott attributes much of the progress to early childhood education, funding for multilingual learners, and college and career readiness pathways.

title: Not all heroes wear capes: Character Counts celebrates a community of classroom coaches
content: Character Counts of Queen Anne's County honored over 100 dedicated classroom coaches with its annual volunteer appreciation dinner on April 24 at Hyatt Place Kent Narrows. The organization, partnering with QACPS since 1999, celebrates its 25th year in incorporating character lessons to kindergarten through fifth grade classrooms and beyond. Coordinator Melinda Ray recognized the dedication of volunteers like Kimberly Kight and Fred Sheriff, who have made a difference in over 4,200 young citizens' lives this school year.

title: PoliTalks transitions leadership as new era begins at Washington College
content:
Here is a concise summary of the article:

Washington College's PoliTalks transitions leadership with co-presidents Charlotte Schurman and Grace Walsh taking over as new era begins. The club, founded by Stephen Hook and Zach Affeldt, aims to provide a safe forum for political education and conversation. Heather Mizeur delivered a lecture on "Sovereignty" at the Hynson Lounge on April 24, emphasizing the importance of standing in one's own agency and maintaining self-control during disagreements. Schurman and Walsh plan to continue PoliTalks' tradition and invite notable speakers, including Serena C. McIlwain, Maryland secretary of the environment.

title: Assanis to step down as University of Delaware president
content: University of Delaware President Dennis Assanis will step down at the end of the school year, citing a desire to make a leadership transition with the institution's best interests in mind. Assanis' one-year contract was due to expire June 30. The board of trustees plans to announce an interim president later, while searching for a new permanent leader through a process that typically takes over a year.

title: A dream come true: Italian exchange student spending a year in Maryland
content: Emma Agazzani, a 17-year-old Italian exchange student from Mantua, Italy, will spend a year in Maryland as part of the American Scandinavian Student Exchange program. She was accepted in February 2022 and is currently attending Huntingtown High School. Agazzani has been able to experience cheerleading, lacrosse, and other extracurricular activities not available in Europe. She plans to study science in college, potentially becoming a neurologist, after completing her secondary education in Italy.

title: KCHS students explore STEM careers with local businesses
content: Kent County High School students participated in a STEM job shadowing program with eight local businesses, including Chesapeake CNC and University of Maryland Shore Medical Center. Zane Carter has supported the program for 13 years, while participating businesses included DMS & Associates and Modern Stone Age Food Lab. The program allows employers to outline educational requirements and real-world demands to students planning their futures.

title: Talbot council mulling $1.1 million request from school district
content:
Here is a concise summary of the article in 4 sentences:

Talbot County Council considers a $1.1 million request from Talbot County Public Schools for fiscal year 2026, including $600,000 for new positions and $500,000 for teacher salary increases. The district's previous request was $5.7 million. County leaders are weighing the best option as they prepare to vote on final amendments to the county's draft $161 million budget on May 27. Talbot County is already mandated by the state to pay $440,000 for teachers' pensions and has considered three potential tax supplement scenarios.

title: Lockerman Middle School Committee previews two sites for new location
content: The Lockerman Middle School Committee previewed two potential new locations and a third option of staying at the current location on May 14, 2025. The first location is behind North Caroline High School, and the second is on Double Hills Road in Denton. Community members expressed concerns and suggestions for both sites, including incorporating historic value into the new school and addressing safety issues. A public meeting will be held on June 2 to gather more feedback before a decision is made by the Board of Education on July 1.

title: 100 years and counting: Talbot County Free Library endures as community linchpin
content: Talbot County Free Library opened in Easton on October 15, 1925, with an 800-book collection founded by Caroline Burnite Walker. The library has adapted to societal changes over the years and now serves residents across the county with over 130,000 books, computer access, and free programs. Executive Director Dana Newman believes the library will continue to evolve and serve the community's needs for years to come.

title: Caroline County schools celebrate teachers
content: Caroline County Public Schools honored teachers and support staff during Teacher Appreciation Week in May 2025. The week featured free coffee and visits from district employees at each school. Caroline County Board of Education President Michele Wayman emphasized the importance of recognizing educators' dedication and hard work. Danielle Dennis, 2024-25 Teacher of the Year, was a math teacher at Colonel Richardson High School and said she became a teacher to make a difference in her community. Amy Bauman, Educators Association President, reflected on the challenges faced by teachers and highlighted their role in inspiring students.

title: Removal of Safe Space stickers draws criticism
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

Melissa Goshorn requested that Superintendent Andraé Townsel remove "Safe Space" stickers from school buildings, citing concerns raised at a National School Boards Association conference. The stickers were removed and drew criticism, with 19 of 20 speakers opposing their removal during a May 8 meeting. Calvert County School Board President Jana Post defended the sticker's removal as not violating First Amendment rights. A motion to discuss a flag policy was unanimously passed, with Marc Watson appointed as supervisor of health, physical education, and athletics.

title: A better life: Local kids on why America is beautiful
content: Helena Sanchez, a third-grade student from Galena Elementary School, won first place in the American Legion Auxiliary's annual Americanism Essay Contest with an essay on what "America the Beautiful" means to her regarding veterans and military. The contest was held at C. Henry Price II, American Legion Post 246 on May 5th, where President of the Auxiliary Patti Bone announced the winners. Other winners included Chloe Cummings (second in third grade) and Liam Miller (first in fifth grade). Winners received cash prizes, certificates, and patriotic items, with the first-place winner also receiving a $50 donation to the Children of Warriors National Presidents' Scholarship fund.

title: Robbins YMCA opening reading hub to tackle childhood illiteracy
content: The Robbins YMCA is opening a reading hub with the John and Janice Wyatt Foundation to tackle childhood illiteracy in Dorchester County, Maryland. The campaign aims to target childhood illiteracy from birth to age 5, partnering with schools, libraries, and community organizations like Operation Pathways. The reading hub will be open to the public and YMCA members, featuring a resource center, community meetings, and parent-teacher sessions. The initiative follows significant budget cuts to Dorchester County Public Schools, which ranked 21st in third-grade literacy and 22nd in overall English Language Arts proficiency.

title: Girl Scout project receives two paws up
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Girl Scout Troop 10069 junior members Sarah Mack, Kait Larson, Greta Isom, and Stella Hageman received a Bronze Award for their project "Pet Friendly Patios in Our Community." The project involved creating maps and decals indicating pet-friendly patios at Leonardtown eateries and cafes. The map is available online and on social media, while decals adorn the front doors of four local businesses. The project took around three months to complete and cost approximately $125.

title: It's time to pause state's education blueprint
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

The Blueprint for Maryland's Future (Kirwan) faces challenges in achieving its goals, including expanding pre-kindergarten participation and funding for schools with high poverty concentrations.
Maryland lags behind 17 other states in enrolling kids in public pre-kindergarten programs, despite spending more per child than previously.
Governor Moore projects a $1 billion structural budget deficit by next year and a $3 billion deficit in fiscal 2027 due to Kirwan funding needs.
The state's fiscal outlook was downgraded to "negative" by Moody's, citing looming structural deficits and the need for bipartisan dialogue on revising Kirwan.
A special legislative session is recommended to pause state funding for Kirwan until a future date and to prevent new mandates for local school boards.

title: TCPS cuts back on summer school; board displeased with how decision was made
content: Talbot County Public Schools cut summer school programs for elementary and middle school students, citing a $350,000 cost. The decision was made without involving the Board of Education, sparking displeasure among board members. Summer school will continue in other forms, including credit recovery for high school students and special education services.

title: Chesapeake College honors Class of 2025
content: Chesapeake College honored its Class of 2025 with a commencement ceremony on May 21, 2025. President Clifford Coppersmith welcomed graduates to new horizons and emphasized hard work and connections. Former U.S. Sen. Ben Cardin received the Community Service Award for his advocacy and dedication to education. Cherie Patchett was awarded the Adjunct Innovative Teaching Award for her innovative teaching methods, while Cianni A. Phillips received the John T. Harrison Award for her leadership and empathy.

title: Students share what America means to them
content: American Legion Auxiliaries celebrated winners of the Americanism essay contest on May 8 in Queenstown, Maryland, recognizing students including Kaleb Brewer, Cash McQuay, and Piper Waldman as national winners. Local students also won awards from posts 296, 278, and 18, with district winners Sydney Kreis and Cole Euler from post 278. The auxiliary heads praised the hardworking students, supportive parents, and teachers for their efforts in participating in the optional national program.

title: 2 TCPS seniors win Service Star awards
content: Kirn Khan and Alexandria Rockwell won Talbot County Public Schools Senior Service Stars awards for their community service. Khan accumulated over 450 hours, while Rockwell completed over 380 hours, volunteering at various organizations such as St. Michaels Community Center and STEM Camp. Both seniors will attend college in the fall: Khan to the University of Maryland on a full scholarship, and Rockwell to the U.S. Naval Academy.

title: Community rallies around retired teacher after tornado
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

Dan Hortert's home in Galestown, Delaware was severely damaged by an EF-1 tornado on May 27, 2025. The community rallied around him with volunteers arriving to help with tractors, cranes, and homemade treats. The damage was mainly caused by two trees, but the family and their cat were unharmed, having sought shelter under the staircase during the storm. Community members, including North Dorchester High School students and staff, came forward to offer support after hearing about the tornado on the day after it hit.

title: Maryland school district delves into AI, conduct codes, cheating
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Cecelia Lewis, director of student services, presented proposed changes to Calvert County public school system's code of conduct, including guidelines for the use of artificial intelligence (AI). The proposed code includes definitions of "academic dishonesty/cheating" that now include unauthorized use of AI-generated materials and utilizing AI to harass or bully. Board members discussed plans for AI training for teachers and students, with an artificial intelligence course for teachers being developed. The revised code will be posted online for public review until late June. A Patuxent High School theatre group, the Harlequins, received a citation from the school board for earning superior scores at the 2025 Maryland Thespians Festival.

title: Rocketeers explode onto the scene at nearby farm
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

The Maryland Delaware Rocketry Association Inc. launched rockets at Central Sod Farm in Centreville on May 17, 2025, following safety guidelines set by the FCC and Tripoli Rocket Association. Hobbyists, including members of the Yorktown Aerospace Club and youth from local communities, launched various types of rockets, with some reaching altitudes of over 1,000 feet. The event was a learning opportunity for students in Science Technology Engineering Mathematics field, with many attendees being introduced to the hobby by experienced rocketeers.

title: Saints Peter and Paul seniors become alumni
content: Sts. Peter and Paul High School's Class of 2025 graduates became alumni by shaking hands with Bishop William Koenig at a ceremony on May 28, 2025, in Easton, Maryland. Associate Pastor Michael Angeloni led prayers, while Senior Class President Francesca Villano shared memories of her classmates' experiences. The graduating class of 49 students received diplomas and artistic awards.

title: Mt. Aviat alumnae gather for first reunion in 40 years
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

Mt. Aviat alumnae gathered for their first reunion in 40 years at Schaefer's Canal House in Chesapeake City on May 30, 2025. The school, which was established from 1960 to 1972 as a girls-only boarding and day high school, was led by Sister Francis Marguerite and Sister Mary Beth. The alumnae reminisced about their experiences at the school, including a notable incident where students were punished for breaking the rules by cleaning the floors with steel wool. The reunion showcased the lasting camaraderie among the former students, who formed close relationships that extend beyond their time at Mount Aviat.

title: Dorchester graduates go off to write their own stories
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

Cambridge-South Dorchester High School and North Dorchester High School seniors accepted their diplomas in Dorchester County on Wednesday and Thursday. Class of 2025 graduates include Salutatorian Elaina Jones, Valedictorian Isabelle Hughs, and twins Julieanne Tobat and Madison Tobat. The class consists of 177 North Dorchester and 214 Cambridge-South Dorchester seniors who will pursue various paths such as college, the workforce, and military service. Graduation speakers included City Council Commissioner Sputty Cephas, Principal Jerome Stover, and teacher Jolene South.

title: Easton, St. Michaels high schools celebrate graduates
content: Easton High School and St. Michaels High School graduates celebrated their achievements with seniors from both schools marking the end of a four-year chapter. 291 graduated from Easton High on Wednesday, while 60 seniors at St. Michaels High School graduated on Thursday. Valedictorian Mia Mazzeo from Easton High emphasized human connections as vital in an AI-driven world, and valedictorian Alexandria Rockwell encouraged her classmates to maintain their drive after graduation.

title: A day for children at the library
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

The Talbot County Free Library will host its 10th annual Chesapeake Children's Book Festival on June 7. The festival will feature 22 children's book authors and illustrators, and attendees can receive a free cookie and voucher for a signed book. The event will also include various activities, such as a story walk and crafts, provided by the library, Maryland State Opera Bears, and other organizations. This year's festival is sponsored by the Friends of the Library, among others.

title: 'Green School' programs in Caroline County bring joy to students
content: Two Caroline County public schools, Denton Elementary and Greensboro Elementary, have been certified as Green Schools by the Maryland Association for Environmental and Outdoor Education. The certification process took two years to complete and involved collaboration with community partners, including organizations such as Pickering Creek Audubon Center and Chesapeake Bay Foundation. Both schools have implemented projects aimed at reducing waste, conserving energy, and promoting sustainability, such as composting programs and garden initiatives. Green Schools certified since 2021, both schools aim for every school to obtain certification.
