title: Colonel Richardson
content: Colonel Richardson graduates from Naval Academy on June 2, 2025, with a class of over 140 cadets including Austin Abrams, Alejandro Alfaro Cruz, Adan Alvi, and others. The graduates hail from various locations, including Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and California. No specific details about Colonel Richardson's name, background, or future plans were provided in the article.

title: St. Michaels
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Stevin Lee, a 65-year-old man from St. Michaels, was killed on June 2, 2025, according to reports by the Star Democrat newspaper. The victims listed include 18 individuals who were allegedly involved with him. No further information is available.

title: North Dorchester
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 sentences:

Hannah Allen and Thomas Allen were killed in a car accident on June 2, 2025, according to a Star Democrat news document. Ty'Ron Anderson and Kaden Andrews are among 67 students listed as survivors of the crash. The victims were from North Dorchester County in Maryland.

title: Lockerman Middle School Committee heard and addressed concerns at second meeting
content: The Lockerman Middle School Committee heard and addressed concerns at its second meeting on June 3, 2025. Architect Robyn Toth confirmed that the current building cannot be renovated due to state assessment results, and it will become a community center. The committee presented two new location options for a new school: one behind North Caroline High School and the other on Double Hills Road in Denton.

title: Caroline County graduations highlight memories and futures
content:
Caroline County's high schools held graduations on May 28-29. 
Colonel Richardson High School graduates included 143 seniors who heard from keynote speaker Danielle Dennis and valedictorian Wilson Clough.
North Carolina High School had 274 graduates, including 10 sets of twins, who watched speeches by keynotes Marnie Stockman and valedictorians Issabelle Greeno, Elizabeth Knott, and Nadelyn Porter.

title: Trump wiped out 75 years of science leadership
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

In 2023-2024, approximately 1.1 million foreign students were studying at US universities, contributing $38 billion annually to the education system. The Trump administration revoked student visas for thousands of international students, including Mahmoud Khalil and Rumeysa Ozturk, who were accused of peaceful protesting against the war in Gaza. This move may lead to a brain drain, as foreign students and researchers consider leaving due to the withdrawal of funds and academic freedom, threatening US leadership in medical science research and other sciences. The US has won 72 Nobel Prizes in science since 2000, with immigrants winning about 30%, and a loss of scientific leadership could have significant economic impacts on states such as California, Texas, Illinois, Massachusetts, New York, and Maryland.

title: Stroke of pen loses 75 years of science leadership
content: The US higher education system may lose $38 billion annually if foreign students are driven away by the Trump administration's revocation of student visas. In 2023-2024, 1.1 million foreign students studied in the US, supporting 378,000 academic jobs. Secretary Marco Rubio planned to expel 300 students, and thousands were initially informed that their visas would be revoked before being restored with a six-day delay. The US is at risk of losing its leadership in medical science research due to potential funding cuts from institutions like Harvard University, the National Institutes of Health, and the National Science Foundation.

title: Suicide of a superpower
content: Max Boot wrote a column in The Washington Post stating that Trump's cost-cutting measures on universities and research programs are causing "suicide of a superpower." Trump is cutting funding for institutions like Princeton University, Columbia University, and the University of Chicago, where scientists like Albert Einstein worked on developing the atomic bomb. These institutions have contributed to significant technological advancements, including satellite radio, smartphones, and internet development.

title: North Caroline grad celebrating more than a high school diploma
content: Sa'Mauria Ennals graduated from North Caroline High School and simultaneously completed an advanced transfer certificate from Chesapeake College and became a certified nursing assistant. She maintained high GPAs at both schools and plans to attend Towson University starting in the fall. Ennals faced challenges getting enrolled in courses but eventually worked with TRIO Upward Bound program coordinators, including Gabrilla Moreland and Mark Berry, to prove her abilities.

title: Massive lunch debt pressures school district
content: The Charles public school system is facing a projected $640,000 lunch debt, with meal funding ending in pandemic, leading to an unplanned $5.7 million budget transfer across various categories. Chief Financial Officer Karen Acton and Budget Manager Sherri Fisher-Davis detailed the reallocation of funds during a June 10 meeting. The school system did not respond for more information by deadline.

title: Book festival gets kids reading
content: The North East Branch Library's annual Children's Book Festival drew over 1,000 attendees on June 20, 2025, despite rain and air quality concerns causing a move indoors. The event featured children's authors including Annette Whipple, who said enthusiasm remained high despite the change in venue. Over 1,000 families received free books upon arrival, while activities such as magic shows, facepainting, and musical performances were also available.

title: MidShore Meals til Monday launches summer meals program for kids
content: MidShore Meals til Monday launched its summer meals program for kids in Cambridge on June 23, targeting child hunger in Dorchester County. The program aims to provide meal boxes for each child per household, containing seven complete breakfasts and lunches, from June 23 to Aug. 21. Partially funded by No Kid Hungry and Preston Automotive, the initiative provides support after Dorchester County Board of Education cut afterschool and summer programs due to a $5.59 million deficit in fiscal year 2026.

title: Foundation of HOPE's new building to expand middle school girls program
content: The Foundation of HOPE plans to build a 5,200-square-foot, two-story building in Easton, MD on South Washington Street for its middle school girls program. The project, valued at $2.2 million, aims to provide a dedicated space for after-school classes and activities. Keasha Haythe, founder and president of the organization, believes the new building will improve the experience for students, including increased accessibility and more resources. Construction could begin as soon as September 2025.

title: Olde School Builders welcomes student apprentice
content: Olde School Builders welcomed Kimberly Escalante-Garcia as its first apprentice on June 16, 2025. Escalante-Garcia, a rising senior at North Caroline High School, was chosen after showing initiative to pursue the apprenticeship after attending a Junior Achievement Fair. Eric Cook, coordinator of career readiness for Caroline County Public Schools, said it was a display of Escalante-Garcia's initiative and ambition. Olde School Builders President Craig Postlewait expressed excitement to have her join the team, which aims to empower girls and young women in the construction industry.

title: Shoe drive will start Greensboro Elementary students off on the right foot
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

St. Paul's United Methodist Church, Greensboro Elementary, and the Town of Greensboro partnered to start a shoe drive for students. The initiative was conceived by Rev. Bonnie Shively as a way to serve the community. New shoes from sizes 7 toddler to size 6 adults are being accepted until August 29. Residents can drop off new shoes at Greensboro Town Hall between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday.

title: Ed Spec Committee recommends North Caroline site for new Lockerman Middle
content: The Caroline County Board of Education recommends North Caroline High School site for new Lockerman Middle School due to infrastructure advantages and shared spaces for events. The proposed location is expected to save $500,000 in development costs compared to Double Hills Road site. The new middle school project budget would be $103.82 million, with state funding covering around $80 million and local funding the remainder.

title: Dorchester schools prepare for more cuts
content: Dorchester County Public Schools face federal funding cuts of over $642,000 due to Trump Administration's decision to withhold $6.8 billion in education funding. The cuts impact teacher training, internal and external student experiences, and English Language Learner programs. Dorchester County faced a budget deficit of $10.19 million in January, which was reduced to $5.59 million by March 2025.

title: Dorchester school board adjusts spending in wake of federal budget cuts
content:
Here is a summary of the article:

The Dorchester County Board of Education met on July 11, 2025, to discuss federal budget cuts affecting $642,000 in funding. The board approved several contracts and programs, including writing instruction, learning software, health department contracts, and facilities improvements, while rejecting Lexia literacy program due to concerns over effectiveness and cost.

title: Moving to the music
content: Ten students from Ashton Mooday's modern band camp in Chestertown recorded their choice song "Best Day of My Life" at Washington College's studio on June 27, 2025. The recording was made possible through a grant by Ken Schweitzer, associate chair of the Department of Music at Washington College, and allowed students to see behind the making of music.

title: DORCHESTER BOARD OF EDUCATION/July 11
content:
The Dorchester Board of Education met on July 11 and approved: 
A $50,000 contract with Houghton Mifflin Harcourt for grades 6-12 for five years. 
An IXL subscription based program for grades 3-12, with a split payment schedule. 
Discontinuing the Lexia contract due to data accuracy concerns. 
Purchasing yearly consumable math materials from Imagine Learning at $113,000.

title: Dorchester County Board of Education discusses student devices
content: The Dorchester County Board of Education is revisiting its student device usage policy due to ineffectiveness of a pilot program implemented last October at three DCPS middle schools. The board voted to get rid of pouches, which students were unable to circumvent, and plan an alternative solution such as locking devices in lockers or backpacks. A final decision will be made on August 21, 2025.

title: Talbot Board of Education/July 16
content: The Talbot County Board of Education approved a new strategic plan on July 16. The board also introduced policy updates on employee code of conduct and video recording in schools. Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones discussed narrowing down retirement plan options from seven to one, with finalists to be interviewed in August and potentially implemented this October. The district reviewed data from the 2024-2025 school year and heard an update on the construction of a staff health center expected to finish by September.

title: Washington College receives $4.5 million gift
content: Richard and Tara Wood have made a $4.5 million gift to Washington College in Chestertown, Maryland. The gift includes funding for endowed chairs in leadership ($2.5 million) and international business ($750,000), as well as an indoor tennis facility ($1 million) and the sailing program ($250,000).

title: 'Closing gaps': TCPS data shows some literacy, math improvements
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

Talbot County Public Schools' test score data from the 2024-2025 school year shows improvements in math and English literacy for some students, particularly Black and Hispanic students. The percentage of kindergarten students scoring above the 50th percentile in math increased to 68% in the 2024-2025 school year. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi attributes the gains to improved curriculum and teacher dedication. Pepukayi aims to address ongoing trends by focusing on the elementary-to-middle transition and hiring reading and math coaches for middle schools.

title: Hip-Hop meets High Street
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Washington College's Starr Center for the Study of the American Experience and the Kohl Gallery partnered with Minary's Dream Alliance to host a two-week summer course called the Hip Hop Time Capsule at Chestertown's innovation plant. The program, which began July 14, 2025, brought together high school students from Cecil, Queen Anne's, and Kent counties, along with college interns, to research and document local African American music history through hip-hop creation. Pat Nugent led the class for the fifth year, while Darius Johnson oversaw the project's development. The program concluded on July 25, 2025, with a special event attended by nearly 100 students from Horizons of Kent and Queen Anne's program.

title: Talbot, Kent see rise in student homelessness
content: Kent County and Talbot County in Maryland saw the largest year-to-year increase in student homelessness, with Kent County's numbers jumping 55% to 102 students and Talbot County's increasing by 39% to 324 students. The Eastern Shore districts of Dorchester (3.6%), Queen Anne's (2.9%), and Caroline (2.2%) reported lower rates. Nonprofit shelters on the Eastern Shore, such as Talbot Interfaith Shelter and His Hope Ministries, are seeing an increase in calls for assistance, with difficulties in serving older youth without guardianship or family support.

title: Washington College opens up pub on campus
content: Washington College has opened The Golden Goose, a pub on campus in Hynson Lounge downstairs, as part of its liquor license approved by Kent County Commissioners on February 25, 2025. The establishment will be restricted to students aged 21 and older, with signs posted stating no one under 21 can enter or bring outside alcoholic beverages. Washington College staff have assured authorities they will check IDs and use wristbands or stamps for age verification. The pub is not open to the public but allows two guests per student.

title: Lockerman High School celebrates 95th anniversary
content:
Here is a concise summary of the article:

Lockerman High School celebrated its 95th anniversary on July 29, 2025. The event was themed "Capturing our history, preserving our legacy and advancing our future." Joseph H. Lockerman High School started in 1930 and remained open until it closed as a Black high school in 1966. The Lockerman name was restored in 1993. The Lockerman Schools Association Inc. presented scholarships to students pursuing higher education and recognized classes with anniversaries from 1935, 1945, 1955, and 1965.

title: Green thumbs: Kids, teens learn to grow plants nature's way
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Wayne Gilchrest, former U.S. Rep., and experts from the University of Maryland Extension are teaching kids in Kent County's summer program to grow plants using natural methods. The program, on county-owned land in Turner's Creek, uses compost piles and mulch mixture donated by local farmers. Kids learn about photosynthesis, soil health, and identifying beneficial insects. The program has been running for its second year with aims to expand and may add a solar-powered well.

title: Board of Ed selects North Caroline site for new Lockerman Middle
content: Caroline County Board of Education members unanimously voted to select the North Caroline High site for the new Lockerman Middle School on August 5, 2025. The site allows for 15.52 acres of space for the new middle school and is located next to North Caroline High School. This location will also enable sharing of space for events with the high school, reducing costs. Board members discussed concerns about a solar array on the property but noted it could be purchased from Tesla for approximately $180,000.

title: Caroline County Board of Education/ Aug. 5
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

Caroline County Board of Education presented a $1,450 check to the Caroline County Public Library through its Imagination Library program on August 5. William Gray was appointed as the district's new supervisor of instruction for physical education. The board approved a five-year produce contract with Teddy Bear Fresh Produce and Keany Produce as vendors. Danielle Dennis, 2024-25 Teacher of the Year, gave a presentation to the board, while the new Lockerman Middle School site will be located at North Caroline High.

title: 'Meeting of the hearts': Women to Watch panelists share advice on mindfulness
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

Women from the Mid-Shore gathered at The Market at Dover Station for the third annual Summer Speaker Series on mindfulness. Panelists Anne Altvater, Morgan Foster, Shania Gregory, and Amber McGinnis shared tips on mindfulness, including letting emotions be present and avoiding technology while stopped at a red light. The event was hosted by APG Chesapeake and moderated by Cassandra Vanhooser. A second panel is scheduled for August 14 at White Oak Manor in Cecil County, and this year's panelists will select their successors for the 2026 Summer Speaker Series.

title: New learning center in southern Maryland provides resources for children with autism
content: SPARKS ABA opened a learning center in Waldorf, Maryland in May for children with autism, offering personalized therapy treatments and multi-learning instruction. The center provides a space for social interaction and peer relationships, with programs aiming to change the trajectory of a child's learning over six-month increments. SPARKS ABA serves 30 Charles County families, using applied behavioral analysis-based services that focus on individual needs. The center offers a range of activities, including zip-glide slides, shelves with toys, and arts and crafts.

title: 'Horses are my happy place': Horse rescue welcomes student readers
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

Morgan Chambers, a 9-year-old student at Calvert Elementary, participated in "Read to the Animals," a program where students read books to retired horses at Freedom Hill Horse Rescue in Owings, MD, on August 12, 2025. The program is part of a partnership between Calvert public schools and Freedom Hill, with an aim to improve reading fluency and animal comfort while promoting service and compassion. Founded 21 years ago, Freedom Hill Horse Rescue welcomes students from kindergarten to fifth-grade for the "Read to the Animals" program, which has been well-received by both children and horses. The initiative is expected to inspire some participants to consider volunteering at the rescue center when older.

title: Caroline County Public Schools welcomes 40 new teachers
content: Caroline County Public Schools welcomed 40 new teachers on August 15, 2025, at a breakfast and orientation event. New assistant principals and a supervisor of instruction were also introduced. Superintendent Derek Simmons emphasized the district's motto "One Family — One Vision." Michele Wayman described CCPS as a "small school system doing big things."

title: For All Seasons school supplies fair moved indoors
content: For All Seasons' annual School Supplies Giveaway and Resource Fair has been moved indoors to Easton Middle School due to rain on August 20, 2025. The event was originally scheduled for Idlewild Park. Katie Theeke, chief marketing and communications officer at For All Seasons, partners with the Talbot County Department of Social Services.

title: How will Talbot County schools regulate AI this year?
content: Talbot County schools outlined new guidelines on artificial intelligence use for the 2025-26 school year. Director of Teaching and Learning Robin Werner presented guidelines at a Board of Education meeting on August 20, 2025. The guidelines include encouraging responsible AI tool use by staff, prohibiting classroom decisions, safe procedures for students, and prohibited uses of AI.

title: Talbot school officials discuss AI guidelines for students, teachers
content: Talbot County school officials discussed AI guidelines for students and teachers at a Board of Education work session on August 20, 2025. Director of teaching and learning Robin Werner presented an AI guidelines document to be observed this school year, emphasizing human oversight is necessary. The guidelines aim to empower students and staff while maintaining academic integrity and equity. Werner noted the State Department of Education lags behind other states in creating AI rules, recommending waiting for state updates before revising official policies.

title: Backpack fair provides hundreds of kids with school supplies
content: Hundreds of backpacks stuffed with school supplies were handed to families ahead of the first day of school at Easton Middle School's indoor resource fair. The event was hosted by For All Seasons and saw over 25 community organizations participate. 800 backpacks were prepared for distribution, which will also be delivered to local schools for those not picked up in person. Carly Palmer, outreach coordinator, said the giveaway helps equip families with supplies throughout the year, while Beth Anne Dorman stated it makes students more confident on day one of school.

title: As students return, Chapel District Elementary begins next phase of renovations
content: Chapel District Elementary School in Cordova, Maryland is set to welcome students next week after completing its renovations. The $27 million project includes adding 16,000 square feet and will be fully finished by 2026. Construction teams completed the second phase of the project this summer, including the school cafeteria and some classrooms, led by Whiting-Turner Contracting Company. Principal Kari Clow reported a smooth staff return earlier in the week. The school's gym is not ready for opening and will reopen by September.

title: Back to school: Talbot celebrates teachers, staff ahead of school year
content: Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi addressed teachers and staff before the annual opening day rally on August 22, 2025, at Easton High School. Pepukayi unveiled new district initiatives, including a "community bus" for providing needs to families and a new early learning center at White Marsh Elementary School in Trappe. Pepukayi also recognized employees with awards, including 2025-26 Talbot Support Staff of the Year Giovanni Wynn and Teacher of the Year Lauren Rose.

title: Dorchester schools seek to curb student violence
content:
Here is a concise summary of the article in 2-5 sentences:

Dorchester County Public Schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson and founders Rebecca Redmer and Phil Whitelock are piloting Risk Threat Crisis' Violence Prevention Initiative at North Dorchester High School to combat student violence. The initiative aims to reduce youth violence, strengthen communication, and build collaboration among schools and communities. The program is being held back by financial constraints but will begin courses in September regardless of funding status. Thompson has struggled with a $10.19 million deficit and is seeking multiple funding streams for the program. The initiative's goal is to create a community approach to violence prevention.

title: Dorchester schools restricting cell phone usage
content: Dorchester County Board of Education passed a new policy restricting cell phone usage for students, banning personal electronic devices during the entire school day. The policy was adopted with 38 supporters and 59 who offered suggestions, while seven opponents voiced concerns. The new policy will take effect on Sept. 2. Dorchester Assistant Superintendent Michael Collins and board members acknowledged the public's comments and feedback during the meeting.

title: If we want reading success, we need to invest
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 concise sentences:

Maryland is set to release its 2025 MCAP test scores, which are likely to reflect years of missed investments in reading education since 2013.
State Superintendent Carey Wright has established frameworks and infrastructure for real change, including a pre-K–3 Literacy Policy and a statewide coaching model.
Wright has secured nearly $50 million in federal and private funds, but these investments are time-limited and unsustainable without a permanent state commitment.
To achieve dramatic improvement, Maryland needs to invest more than just hiring the right superintendent, requiring sustained resources from the legislature.

title: Talbot County students return to school
content: Students at Talbot County's eight public schools returned to classrooms on August 25, 2025. The district began its school year earlier than other districts, starting after Labor Day weekend. St. Michaels Elementary Principal Indra Bullock greeted families at car drop-off, while teachers showed kids the way to the front door. Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi announced the implementation of a cell phone pouch policy for St. Michaels Middle School students and emergency lanyards for staff.

title: Back to school: what's ahead for Talbot County classrooms
content: Talbot County classrooms are in session with a new school year bringing fresh opportunities for education coverage. Reporter Konner Metz covered the first day of classes and highlighted two upcoming programs addressing cell phone usage and classroom safety.

title: State test scores: Mid-Shore school districts see mixed results
content:
Here is a concise summary of the article:

Mid-Shore school districts saw mixed results in English and math test scores released by the Maryland Department of Education on August 26, 2025. Dorchester County made significant gains, with English proficiency increasing 7.6% to 41.3%. The district ranked 19th in the state. Queen Anne's County remained the most proficient in math at 31.6%, while Talbot County saw the worst year-to-year decrease in science scores.

title: The results are in, and Dorchester County saw some big gains
content: Dorchester County saw the largest jump in English proficiency among Maryland school districts during the 2024-25 school year, with a significant gain according to test results released on August 27, 2025. The district ranks 19th out of 24 in English proficiency. Superintendent Jymil Thompson attributed the improvement as progress towards climbing state rankings.

title: Cellphone pouches are back in Caroline County middle schools
content: Caroline County Public Schools will bring back cellphone pouches in middle schools for a second year, following a successful pilot program introduced in the 2024-25 school year. The company Yondr created the pouches, and they were tested in both Caroline County middle schools last year. The first year saw 30.6% fewer referrals, 130 fewer attacks or fights, and 200 fewer instances of disrespect and disruptions. Superintendent Derek Simmons said student and parent receptivity improved over time, with minimal resistance to the program's compliance.

title: Constitution Bowl contest is coming to Easton
content: The Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance hosts the U.S. Constitution Scholastic Competition on Sept. 20 at the Talbot County Free Library, in partnership with the Colonel Tench Tilghman Chapter of the Sons of the American Revolution. The event is part of several activities during Constitution Week (Sept. 14-20), including a recognition ceremony on Constitution and Citizenship Day (Sept. 17). Competing teams from local schools will earn community recognition and prizes.

title: Dorchester schools climb in state rankings after first year of ambitious reform plan
content: Dorchester County Public Schools Superintendent Jymil Thompson's "23, no more" initiative aims to move DCPS from 23rd to 15th in Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program evaluations. After a year of reform, testing data shows the district moved up two spots overall and improved English Learning Arts proficiency from 23rd to 19th. The district's strategic plan "Believe in Us" guides efforts with priorities including advance academics, optimize operations, pursue partnerships, and cultivate conversations. Thompson hopes to recruit more teachers and administrators to improve the school system's attractiveness and act as a catalyst for countywide transformation.

title: Federalsburg Judy Center celebrates 25 years
content: Federalsburg Judy Center Hub celebrated 25 years of operation in August 2025, offering early intervention and comprehensive services to families with children ages 5 and younger at Federalsburg Elementary School. Heather Harding is the coordinator, while Elizabeth Saylor is the supervisor of instruction. The center has partnered with community agencies since its inception, promoting school readiness through collaboration with Caroline County Public Schools.

title: First day of school madness
content: Lily Tierney wrote about the first day of school in Dorchester County on September 2, 2025. The article featured her own experience covering the event at Denton Elementary School, where students greeted teachers and administrators after hopping off their yellow school bus. Her colleague Ahmad was initially scheduled to cover Caroline County's first day of school but encountered traffic issues.

title: Students head back to school in Caroline County
content: Students in Caroline County began their first day of school on September 2, 2025, at Denton Elementary School. Superintendent Derek Simmons and other school officials greeted students as they arrived by yellow buses. Parents watched proudly as children entered the school for the first time this year. Students, including second-grader and fourth-grader DeAndre Ryan's sons, were excited to see their friends again.

title: Flag day: Maryland academy welcomes ambassador from Guinea
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Madam Sidibe Fatoumata Kaba, Ambassador from Guinea, visited West Nottingham Academy in Colora on September 2, 2025, to accept a flag representing her country as part of the school's collection. The addition marks strengthening cultural relations between the US and Guinea in higher education. There are three Guinean students at WNA this year. Kaba called it an honor to witness the flag-raising ceremony near Rising Sun and Port Deposit.

title: Caroline schools outline funding plan for new Lockerman Middle in capital improvement program
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 4 sentences:

Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Derek Simmons presented the fiscal year 2027 capital improvement program to the Board of Education on September 2. The plan allocates $1.4 million for Lockerman Middle School's new location in FY27, increasing to $8.1 million in FY28 and $15.5 million in FY29. Simmons expects state funding to be lowered over time due to projections. The county and state will negotiate the allocation amounts, with the hope of meeting a "middle ground".

title: CAROLINE COUNTY BOARD OF EDUCATION/ Sept. 2, 2025
content: On September 2, 2025, the Caroline County Board of Education approved a five-year capital improvement program of $103 million and a staffing update that showed a fully staffed school system with only three instructional assistant vacancies. The board also approved an overnight field trip to the National Convention and new facilities projects totaling $111,000. Preston Elementary added a fishbowl window and implemented conscious discipline, while Colonel Richardson Middle School installed a new roof and implemented positive behavioral interventions and supports.

title: KIHS' Mamas named among finalists for Maryland Teacher of the Year
content: Marcie Mamas, a business teacher at Kent Island High School in Stevensville, Maryland, is one of seven finalists for the 2026 Maryland Teacher of the Year award. Mamas has taught for 30 years and previously won the Maryland Business Teacher of the Year award. The winner will be announced on September 26, 2025, and compete for the National Teacher of the Year Award in April 2026.

title: Country Cooking: Welcome back to school and school lunches
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

Marie Savage reflects on her school days in Bishopville and shares memories of school lunches in the 1950s to 2025. Schools have changed their lunch options over time, with popular items including spaghetti, submarines, and a la carte foods. In recent years, there has been an increase in allergens such as peanuts, gluten, and dairy, leading to more limited menu options. Savage shares recipes for convenient and affordable packed lunches, including BBQ chicken cups, PB&J apples, and grilled cheese roll-ups.

title: Caroline County school athletic facilities will soon have bathrooms
content: Caroline County Commissioners President Travis Breeding and Public Schools Director of Operations Bill Mengel worked together to add new bathrooms to North Caroline High School and Colonel Richardson High School outdoor athletic facilities since March 2024. The project was included in the county's fiscal year 2025 budget, which was approved by commissioners. The new bathrooms will have separate men's and women's sides with toilets at both high schools, expected to be operational by late September or early October.

title: Gen Z’s lessons on Sept. 11: A generation raised in its shadow calls for deeper lessons
content: Addison Nogar, a junior at Kent Island High School, reflects on the lessons of September 11. In 2013, she saw the film "World Trade Center" and was deeply impacted by its graphic content. She recalls learning about Welles Crowther, a volunteer firefighter who saved over 18 lives in the South Tower before losing his life. Nogar visited the National September 11 Memorial and Museum on April 22, 2023, where she saw the Survivor Tree, a Callery pear tree that survived the attacks.

title: Girls' STEM gains are slipping
content: Girls' STEM gains are declining at a faster rate than boys since the pandemic. Mid-Shore school districts show this trend. A statewide group focused on youth STEM programming was contacted for answers, but district representatives were unresponsive to initial inquiries. The article aims to round out this story with further information.

title: Girls lose gains in math and science post-pandemic
content: Girls' math scores declined by almost an entire grade level in Maryland between 2019 and 2024, with girls falling behind boys by an average of 49% of a grade level more than boys. Girls on Maryland's Eastern Shore, including Talbot, Caroline, and Dorchester counties, followed this trend. The national trend shows girls declining faster than boys in math and science subjects since the pandemic.

title: Easton, St. Michaels victorious in 1st ever Mid-Shore Constitution Bowl
content: Easton High School and St. Michaels High School won the inaugural Mid-Shore Constitution Bowl, hosted by the Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance at the Talbot County Free Library on September 22, 2025. Easton secured the grand prize with 415 points, while St. Michaels took first place in the small division with 265 points. The competition was part of Constitution Week from September 14 to 20, and students attributed their victory to preparation and practice led by former AP Government teacher James Kunz.

title: Who knew the Constitution could be this competitive?
content: A Mid-Shore Constitution Alliance hosted its first-ever Constitution Bowl at the Talbot County Free Library on September 20-22, 2025, featuring high school students from local schools competing in a sporting event-style contest to display their knowledge of the U.S. Constitution. Easton High School and St. Michaels High School won their respective divisions. The event was part of Constitution and Citizenship Week (Sept. 14-20).

title: Queen Anne's denies charter school application
content:
Here is a summary of the article in 2-5 concise sentences:

The Queen Anne's County Public Schools Board of Education voted to deny the application for a classical charter school on September 10, 2025, due to significant deficiencies in academic planning and operational readiness. The charter school group will retain the right to appeal or resubmit during the next application window.

title: Talbot school board dives into test score trends
content: Talbot County school officials examined state test scores for 2024-2025 Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program, showing upward trends in math and English for some grades but dips in others. The results showed increases in English proficiency for third and fourth grades, but drops for fifth and eighth grades. Math proficiency spiked year-to-year for fourth, sixth, and seventh grades, but the number of students proficient in algebra fell significantly. Talbot County's English proficiency dropped to 45.4%, while math proficiency was 18.9%. The district aims to find solutions to address problem areas.

title: Maryland Supreme Court coming to Easton for first time since 1851
content: The Maryland Supreme Court is holding an oral arguments hearing at Easton High School on Friday, October 3, 2025, for two cases: one civil and one criminal. The court will be led by Justice Brynja Booth, who represents the 1st Appellate Judicial Circuit encompassing the Eastern Shore. title: Maryland Supreme Court makes 'unprecedented' trip to Easton
content: The Maryland Supreme Court held oral arguments for two cases at Easton High School on October 3, 2025, a first in 174 years since 1851. title: A day to remember at the library
content: The Talbot County Free Library opened on October 15, 1925, as a community undertaking led by Caroline Burnite Walker and 40 women who pledged $50 each. The library's first librarian was hired in 1924 for $900 a year, with an initial collection of 800 books. The library will celebrate its 100th anniversary on October 16, 2025, with a gala event featuring music by the Julie Parsons Project Jazz Duo and other performances.

The plan aims to provide an effective learning environment and minimize disruptions while preserving school property value and maximizing facility efficiency. title: 'Bring people together': Radio station honoring Harriet Tubman launches in Mid-Shore
content: A new radio station honoring Harriet Tubman's legacy, WFHW 90.3 FM, will launch on October 12, 2025, in Cambridge, MD. The station is a joint effort between WHCP 91.7 FM and the Harriet Tubman Museum and Educational Center. Amanda Tilghman and Linda Harris spearheaded the project, which aims to educate residents about Harriet Tubman's life and legacy. The station will include a five-day-a-week talk show hosted by Harris, as well as programming from WHCP and nationally syndicated shows.

title: Banned books once again increasing
content: Banned Books Week is celebrated for the 43rd year starting October 5-11, 2025, in response to a surge in book challenges since 1982. PEN America reported 6,870 book bans enacted during the 2024-25 school year across 23 states and 87 public school districts. The majority of challenged books are by authors of color, LGBTQ+ authors, women, and focus on racism, sexuality, gender, and history. Libraries saw a 92% increase in challenged titles in 2023, largely driven by organized groups and politicians.

title: Talbot Board of Ed digs into student discipline trends
content: Talbot County Public Schools officials reviewed district data on suspensions and expulsions during a Board of Education work session. According to state regulations, administrators must indicate an "imminent threat" for expulsion, which has not been the case in the last three full school years. The district reported no expulsions or significant out-of-school suspensions so far this year. Talbot County's suspension and expulsion rates are lower than neighboring counties, with 5% of students suspended or expelled in the 2023-2024 school year.

title: Students experience Farm to School eating
content: Teachers and volunteers led students to a field outside Mechanicsville Elementary School, where they experienced Farm to School events. Kaitlin Fraer organized events at three elementary schools in St. Mary's County for National Farm to School Month. The events included stations about farm animals, fruits, vegetables, and healthy eating, with guest speakers Beth Palumbo and Christine Allred. Students also planted sweet potatoes and met farm animals, including a blind horse named Willa.

title: Talbot Board of Ed OKs contracts for EHS auditorium, Chapel Elementary windows
content: The Talbot Board of Education approved contracts for two projects: $1.1 million auditorium lights at Easton High School to be installed in summer 2026, and $132,000 window glazing with security film at Chapel District Elementary School in Cordova, Maryland, expected to be completed this summer.

title: 'This place impacts lives': Talbot County Free Library celebrates 100th birthday
content:
Talbot County Free Library celebrated its 100th birthday on October 17, 2025, with two books missing from the shelves for 50 years being returned by state senator Johnny Mautz.
Caroline Burnite Walker founded the library in 1925.
The library is now a full-fledged community hub offering residents access to books, computers, research rooms, and community events.
Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher reflected on how the library guided his research projects and skills, stating it impacts lives.

title: Empowerment Center offers after-school education
content:

The Cambridge Empowerment Center on Pine Street offers after-school education programs for children from pre-kindergarten to age 13, including arts and crafts, math, art, and IXL learning site. Director Tammy Washington oversees programs with free pre-K available, while after-school programming costs $125 for six weeks and includes meals, field trips, and education. The center opened in 2003 and now operates on grant funding and donations, with staff paid and certified to work with children. The center hosts an open house on Nov. 9 for community members to learn more about its programs and services.

title: Rotarian from Uganda talks about life
content: Robin Kibuka, a Ugandan Rotarian, spoke to the Rotary Club of Cambridge about his life growing up in Uganda and his educational background at Yale University and Harvard University, where he earned a PhD in economics. After working at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Kibuka retired with a focus on giving back, sharing his legacy through books and service work. He emphasized the importance of listening as a leader and improved empathy.
